description: Just a computer engineering student exploring astronomy.
summary:
SPHEREx Blink is a free, public web tool that lets anyone see how the infrared sky changes over time in NASA's SPHEREx all-sky survey. You enter an object name or sky coordinates (or click a one-tap test target such as WISE 0855-0714 or Barnard's Star), and the app gathers every SPHEREx exposure of that patch from NASA/IPAC IRSA, lines them up on a single grid, and plays them like a short video. Stars stay put; comets, asteroids, brown dwarfs and fast-moving stars visibly jump between frames.

It answers the challenge by turning a huge archive into something a person can understand in seconds. Scientists get difference imaging, stacking, star masking, spectra, light curves, Gaia and AllWISE overlays, and a shift/parallax estimator. Newcomers get a plain, classic desktop-style interface with plain-language help and a spectrum they can even hear. Every view is shareable and embeddable by link.

It matters because no one person can sift through more than a billion detected objects alone. Making movement easy to see lets students, citizen scientists and researchers all help spot the unexpected, and new SPHEREx releases can be added with one line of code.
details:
SPHEREx Blink is a web tool for spotting moving objects in NASA's SPHEREx near-infrared survey. SPHEREx maps the whole sky every six months in 102 colours, so the same patch of sky is photographed many times. Stars stay fixed, while comets, asteroids, brown dwarfs and high-proper-motion stars shift between exposures. The app finds every exposure of a chosen position, aligns them, and blinks through them like a short video.

HOW TO USE IT

1. Type an object name (resolved through SIMBAD/NED), enter RA/Dec in degrees or sexagesimal, or click a test target: WISE 0855-0714, Barnard's Star, Epsilon Indi B, RW Aurigae, R Draconis, or positions taken from NASA's own IRSA tutorials (M101, a COSMOS field, a PAH-bright cloud).

2. Choose the field of view (about 2 to 30 arcminutes) and which of the six detector bands to use.

3. Press Blink, or step and scrub through the timeline, which is coloured by band.

HOW IT WORKS

- A Next.js backend queries NASA/IPAC IRSA's SIA service (spherex_qr3 and spherex_dr1 collections) for every spectral image covering the position, then requests small FITS cutouts from IRSA's cutout service. It retries on transient read errors, which IRSA's own tutorials mention.

- Our own FITS reader parses the IMAGE and FLAGS extensions, the WCS with SIP distortion terms, and the wavelength lookup table. Bad pixels are masked from the flag bits, and each frame shows its masked-pixel percentage.

- The browser reprojects every frame onto one north-up grid and renders it on an HTML canvas.

- The FITS parser, coordinate math and wavelength interpolation were checked against astropy on an independent reference file and agree to sub-micro-arcsecond.

FEATURES FOR FINDING MOVERS

- Difference imaging: subtract the per-band median or the previous frame so anything that moves stands out.

- Stacking: coadd same-epoch exposures to raise signal-to-noise.

- Star masking: hide very bright stars by replacing them with the local background, so faint movers are easier to see.

- Gaia DR3 and AllWISE overlays. Gaia positions are moved to each frame's date using proper motion, so a source that does not follow a Gaia track is a candidate mover.

- Proper-motion tracking for the preset stars so fast movers stay centred.

- Shift and distance tool: mark an object in two frames to get its shift, rate, and a rough distance if the shift were pure parallax from Earth's orbit.

FEATURES FOR UNDERSTANDING THE LIGHT

- Click any spot to get a spectrum (brightness versus wavelength) from every loaded exposure, or a light curve (brightness versus date) for variable stars.

- Hear spectrum: plays the spectrum as sound (pitch is wavelength, loudness is brightness), which makes the data accessible to blind and low-vision users.

SHARING AND ACCESS

- The whole state lives in the URL (position, field of view, bands), so any view can be shared. Adding embed=1 gives a clean version for iframes.

- Export the current frame as PNG or the whole blink as a WebM video.

- Keyboard control (space, left and right arrows) and a phone layout.

- A "Real data and docs" page shows real values from NASA's IRSA tutorials: the first channels of a real SPHEREx spectrum, the spectral channel table, test positions, the archive query, and the mission details and acknowledgement text.

- A clearly labelled DEMO mode with simulated data keeps the tool usable if the archive is down.

BENEFITS AND INTENDED IMPACT

- Scientists get a fast first look at a position without writing code.

- Students, teachers and citizen scientists can discover for themselves how things move in space, in the spirit of projects like Backyard Worlds and WiseView.

- There is no database and no separate backend, so it is cheap to host and easy to keep running.

- Updating for a new release is one line (the archive collection name in one file).

WHAT MAKES IT CREATIVE

- Moving Gaia stars to each frame's date means the overlay itself shows which sources are NOT behaving like known stars.

- Turning a spectrum into sound, and a very plain classic desktop look in violet, pink and yellow, so the tool feels friendly instead of intimidating.

- Using the six detector bands as separate, toggleable layers, plus stacking across bands.

DESIGN CHOICES

We designed for two audiences at once: a scientist who wants stretch controls, flags and photometry, and a newcomer who only wants to press one button and see something move. We kept the interface plain and clearly labelled, explained every control in everyday words, and avoided animations that get in the way. We were also upfront about uncertainty: spectra are aperture surface brightness, not calibrated photometry, and the parallax distance is a rough estimate that assumes the whole shift comes from Earth's motion.

TOOLS AND TECHNOLOGY

TypeScript, React and Next.js (API routes proxy the archive and cache responses), HTML canvas for image rendering, the Web Audio API for sound, MediaRecorder for video export, deployed on Vercel with code on GitHub. No special hardware is needed, since it runs in an ordinary browser. We used the Claude AI assistant for coding help and tested the core math against astropy.

DATA

NASA/IPAC IRSA SPHEREx spectral images and cutouts, AllWISE (NASA), Gaia DR3 (ESA) and the CDS VizieR and Sesame services. Full links are listed below.
